newsitem.title: USA: U.S. insurers now see opportunity with banks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. insurers now see opportunity with banks.

text.p: After waging a bitter battle to keep banks from selling insurance, U.S. insurers and agents are now beginning to see the banks as potential partners rather than rivals.

Instead of fighting for the same customrs, insurers and agents may find that they will gain a whole new set of customers -- the banks themselves, according to speakers at a seminar at the Insurance Leadership Forum here.

The banks, which are often unable and unwilling to start up an insurance operation on their own, will turn to insurance industry professionals for advice, expertise and their books of business, the speakers said Monday at the conference, sponsored by the Council of Insurance Agents & Brokers and the Council of Insurance Company Executives.
"The banks can't do this without them (insurance professionals)," William Evenson, a consultant for banking and insurance organizations told Reuters after the seminar.
"They'd be insane to try," he said.
Although banks have been selling insurance products such as annuities for some time, they were unable to sell life and property and casualty insurance.
But earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court decided to allow banks to sell such insurance.
Barnett Banks Inc this week said it was ready to test-market life, auto and homeowners insurance in Tampa and hopes to expand sales statewide early next year.
But banks will have a hard time trying to enter the insurance market with start-up operations of their own, the seminar speakers said.

Without any track record, established market or infrastructure, they will have little advantage over their insurance industry competitors, said Dennis Kosovac, president and chief executive of Chase Manhattan Bank's Chase Insurance Agency Inc.

Bankers also usually have little interest in actually becoming insurance salesmen and see offers to run their bank's fledgling insurance operation as a dead end job, said Patrick Phelan, executive vice president of Dean and Co in Cleveland, Ohio.
"Their secret ambition is not to sell insurance," he told the conference.
Establishing a brand new insurance sales unit also involves considerable time and expense for training and licensing, he said.
This all adds up to opportunities for insurers and agencies. But it also involves potential pitfalls as well, the speakers said.

Agents may find their skills are in demand with the banks, which may be willing to hire them as consultants or to run their new insurance operations, said Kenneth Reynolds, executive director of the Association of Banks-in-Insurance, based in Washington, D.C.
Or, they may find banks willing to make buyout offers or set up strategic alliances to gain access to their expertise and books of business, he told the conference.
Meanwhile, insurers also can gain access to the banks' clientele.
"The success of this (for agents) is that it cuts down on the time prospecting," Evenson said. "If it doesn't cut down on prospecting, then it's not profitable."
But the banking and insurance cultures are so different, the speakers said, that it could result in a clash that could undermine any relationship between the two.
Evenson said he advises insurance agencies to use caution before rushing into a relationship with a bank.
Meanwhile, he said, insurance agencies need not panic about the prospect of banks selling insurance.

"You are not going to get steamrolled by the banks," he said. Insurance still makes up a very small part of the banking industry's overall business and it will take time for the banks to make serious inroads.
"Anything in commercial property and casualty is a ways down the road yet," he said.
